advances: Exact coordinate and measure equivalence. The sharp full-volume assertion is false by the accepted counterexample. The locked weak bound remains a separate open question.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
If $b=0$, scaling an original point along its positive ray leaves its image unchanged. An integer origin translation within the positive chart replaces $b$ by the original positive value of $\ell$ there and preserves the lattice. For $b>0$ the relation $1-a\cdot(z/\ell(z))=b/\ell(z)$ gives the inverse. More generally $b\ne0$ is sufficient before the translation, with image specified by $D/b>0$. The map takes a convex combination $(1-\lambda)p_0+\lambda p_1$ to the convex combination of the image points with weights proportional to $(1-\lambda)\ell(z_0),\lambda\ell(z_1)$. The normalized second weight ranges over $[0,1]$, so both maps preserve segments and hence convexity. Continuity gives compactness for sets contained in the open chart. The inverse tests membership in $\Omega$ by $bu/D(u)\in\mathbb Z^n$, proving relative closedness and discreteness. The segment formula at $\lambda=1/2$, with $\ell(z_j)=b/D_j$, gives the stated midpoint. For example, with $\ell(z)=z+1$ the indices $0,2$ map to $0,2/3$. Their Euclidean midpoint $1/3$ has inverse base $1/2$, while the exact projective midpoint $1/2$ has inverse base $1$.

On each original integer fiber $z$ the continuous map is a homothety of ratio $1/\ell(z)$. Hausdorff measure scales by $\ell(z)^{-q}$, giving the claimed compensating weight, equal to one for $q=0$. The image of a closed cap $\alpha\cdot z+\beta\cdot x\ge c$ has equation $(b\alpha+ca)\cdot u+b\beta\cdot y\ge c$ inside the chart by multiplication by the positive denominator. Conversely coefficients $A,B,c$ in the image come from $\alpha=(A-ca)/b,\ \beta=B/b$. Degenerate inverse equations restrict to the full or empty chart and do not affect an infimum at an eligible point. Thus closed boundaries, centers and cap masses are preserved. If $a\ne0$, choose an integer vector $v$ with $a\cdot v>0$ and translate any original compact body by a sufficiently large multiple of $v$. Translation preserves lattice depth and puts the entire body into this fixed chart. If $a=0$ the chart is already global. This proves the universal equivalence with its quantifiers. In particular the full-volume sharp counterexample 022a26fa5001480a also refutes the weighted sharp assertion by this transport.

For the standard equality example, let $T$ be a $d$-simplex and use $[0,1]^n\times T$. At any fiber centroid the own cap mass is at least $\gamma_d|T|_d$, by baee8ddaa588aef0 (constant containing restrictions capture the whole fiber). At any mark some barycentric coordinate is at least $1/(d+1)$, so its upper vertex cap through the mark has own mass at most $\gamma_d|T|_d$. An affine base tilt isolates it by strictly penalizing every other binary base. Thus the product maximum is exactly $\gamma_d/2^n$ normalized, and its translated image realizes the same maximum.

Brunn–Minkowski on the convex image body gives concavity of $|C'_u|_d^{1/d}=(D(u)/b)m(u)^{1/d}$. Substitute at $u_t$ and use the affinity of $D$ for the ordinary-interpolation formula. With $t=\lambda\ell(z_1)/[(1-\lambda)\ell(z_0)+\lambda\ell(z_1)]$, the normalized weights $(1-t)D_0/D(u_t),\,tD_1/D(u_t)$ become $1-\lambda,\lambda$. The weight itself is log-convex for $d>0$, since its log equals $d\log b-d\log D$.

The corresponding fiber-only division with the base kept fixed can lose both convexity and ambient caps even for $\ell(z)=z+1$ on $z\ge0$. It sends $x\ge1$ to $y\ge1/(z+1)$, which has a curved boundary. The image of $[0,2]\times[0,1]$ contains $(0,1)$ and $(2,1/3)$ but excludes their midpoint $(1,2/3)$ because the image fiber at $1$ ends at $1/2$.

statement:
Let $\ell(z)=a\cdot z+b$ and $F(z,x)=(z,x)/\ell(z)$ on $\ell>0$. If $b=0$ the chart loses scale. If the chart contains an integer base, translate that base to the origin so that $b>0$. Set $D(u)=1-a\cdot u$ and $\Omega=\{z/\ell(z):z\in\mathbb Z^n,\ \ell(z)>0\}$. In these coordinates $F$ maps bijectively onto $D>0$ with inverse $F^{-1}(u,y)=b(u,y)/D(u)$. It preserves convexity and takes compact sets contained in its domain to compact sets. The mixed set becomes $\Omega\times\mathbb R^d$, with $\Omega$ discrete and relatively closed inside $D>0$. If $w_j=F(z_j,x_j)$, $D_j=D((w_j)_{\rm base})$, then the image of the inverse midpoint is $(D_1w_0+D_0w_1)/(D_0+D_1)$. Its base belongs to $\Omega$ whenever $z_0,z_1$ have the same parity.

For summed $q$-dimensional Hausdorff fiber measure, $0\le q\le d$, the pushforward is $\nu(A')=\sum_{u\in\Omega}(b/D(u))^q\mathcal H_q(A'_u)$, for measurable sets in the chart. On a finite positive-mass sample, raw and normalized closed-halfspace depths at every corresponding eligible point are equal. In particular every universal normalized full-volume bound with a fixed constant $\kappa(n,d)$ is equivalent to the same bound for the weighted image bodies of a fixed positive chart. This applies separately to the sharp proposal and to the locked weak bound.

For $d\ge1$ and an actual compact convex image body $C'$, write $m(u)=(b/D(u))^d|C'_u|_d$ on its real base projection. The function $(D(u)/b)m(u)^{1/d}$ is concave. At $u_t=(1-t)u_0+tu_1$ the corresponding lower bound for $m(u_t)^{1/d}$ is $[(1-t)D_0m(u_0)^{1/d}+tD_1m(u_1)^{1/d}]/D(u_t)$. At the projectively reparameterized interpolation the original weights are recovered. For $\ell(z)=z+1$, leaving the base fixed while dividing only the continuous coordinate by $\ell$ can destroy both cap and convex-set geometry.
title: Full projective charts preserve sampled incidence and weighted halfspace depth
